props.title: PT 109

sections.content: PT 109 stands as a unique entry in the WWII naval genre, dramatizing John F. Kennedy's actual wartime experiences while serving as a PT boat commander in the Pacific. Released during Kennedy's presidency, it's a rare instance of a sitting president being portrayed on screen, with Cliff Robertson delivering a measured performance as the young JFK. The film meticulously recreates the famous incident where Kennedy's PT boat was rammed and split in half by a Japanese destroyer, followed by the future president's heroic leadership in saving his crew.

sections.content: The 1960s saw a surge in biographical war films focusing on individual heroism. While PT 109 emphasized Kennedy's leadership, The Great Escape (1963) showcased Steve McQueen in a fictionalized version of a true POW breakout. Lawrence of Arabia (1962) elevated the biographical war film to epic status, with Peter O'Toole embodying T.E. Lawrence's complex character against the backdrop of WWI's Middle Eastern campaign.

Naval warfare films of this era typically balanced action with character development. The Caine Mutiny (1954) explored psychological pressure in command, while In Harm's Way (1965) with John Wayne examined leadership during Pearl Harbor's aftermath. PT 109 fits this pattern but stands apart through its unprecedented portrayal of a sitting president's military service. SUBHEAD: Presidential Portrayal in War Films

sections.content: The unique aspect of PT 109 lies in its timing and subject matter. While other presidents have been portrayed on film, most depictions came years after their terms. Young Mr. Lincoln (1939) and Abe Lincoln in Illinois (1940) portrayed Lincoln's early years, but Kennedy was actively serving as president during PT 109's production and release, creating an unusual intersection of contemporary politics and war film storytelling.
